[← Return to the entropy lesson](entropy.qmd) · [Cross-entropy](cross-entropy.qmd)

## The central idea

A model assigns a probability to the next token. A highly probable observation is unsurprising; a low-probability observation is costly to explain. Information theory turns this intuition into measurable quantities.

## Five formulas to remember

| Quantity | Formula | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Surprisal | \(I(x)=-\log_2 p(x)\) | Information content of an observed event, in bits |
| Entropy | \(H(X)=\mathbb E[-\log p(X)]\) | Average uncertainty of a distribution |
| Cross-entropy | \(H(q,p)=\mathbb E_{x\sim q}[-\log p(x)]\) | Average cost of predicted distribution p on target q |
| KL divergence | \(D_{KL}(q\|p)=\mathbb E_q[\log(q/p)]\) | Non-negative discrepancy between q and p |
| Perplexity | \(\mathrm{PPL}=e^{\mathrm{NLL}}\) | Exponential of mean NLL in nats |

The logarithm base sets the unit: base 2 gives bits; the natural logarithm gives nats.

## The key identity

```text
H(q,p) = H(q) + D_KL(q || p)
```

For a fixed target q and context, H(q) does not depend on model parameters. Minimizing cross-entropy therefore minimizes D_KL(q || p). For a one-hot target, H(q)=0, so cross-entropy is exactly the NLL of the observed token.

## Worked example

For q = (0.5, 0.5) and p = (0.75, 0.25):

- H(q) = 0.693 nats;
- H(q,p) = 0.837 nats;
- D_KL(q || p) = 0.144 nats.

Thus 0.837 ≈ 0.693 + 0.144.

## Connection to compression

A probability p(x) corresponds to an ideal code length close to -log₂ p(x) bits. A good predictor can therefore support shorter codes. For dependent sequences, distinguish marginal entropy from entropy rate. This does not prove compression = intelligence: the measurement depends on corpus, tokenization and coding protocol.

## Three conceptual traps

1. **Entropy is not the surprisal of one token.** Entropy is an average; surprisal concerns one event.
2. **Marginal entropy is not entropy rate.** For dependent sequences, single-symbol frequencies do not capture long-run uncertainty per symbol.
3. **Attention weights are not mutual information.** Attention weights aggregate values; mutual information is defined from a joint distribution.
4. **Landauer is not a universal learning ceiling.** Its bound concerns physical irreversible erasure, not a general limit on generalization.


## Further study — predictive \(\mathcal V\)-information

Predictive \(I_{\mathcal V}(X\to Y)\) measures the prediction gain available to a specified family \(\mathcal V\) under logarithmic loss. It therefore depends on the allowed models. If the family is expressive enough to contain all predictors, it recovers Shannon mutual information; with a restricted family, it may be smaller.

Do not treat it as a new assumption-free quantity: always specify the family, target, side information and loss. See the controlled experiment below.


## Self-check

1. Why is cross-entropy at least as large as target entropy?
2. When does cross-entropy reduce to token NLL?
3. Why does a high attention weight not measure mutual information?

<details>
<summary>Show answers</summary>

1. Their difference is KL divergence, which is non-negative under the usual support conditions.
2. When the target is one-hot: only the probability of the observed token contributes.
3. Attention weights are normalized compatibility coefficients, not a joint distribution or an estimator of statistical dependence.

</details>
